query: An equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy has a simple solid-solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its microstructure and deformation behavior remain insufficiently understood. Under hardness testing and mechanical loading of this starting state, what single intervention could overcome the strength and hardness limitation while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics? State the proposed intervention, its mechanism, the predicted measurable change relative to the unmodified alloy, its applicable processing and test conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a microstructural and mechanical experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of titanium to the CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy can overcome the strength and hardness limitation while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution and nano-sized oxides
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and hardness while maintaining favorable mechanical characteristics
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of titanium to be added and the optimal processing conditions

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of titanium does not result in improved strength and hardness, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
